title: SCARDEC source duration did not predict 30-day aftershock counts of 1,634 shallow Mw 6+ mainshocks (1992-2024); thrust and strike-slip slopes had opposite signs
abstract: Question: do earthquakes with a short source duration for their moment (a high stress-drop proxy) have fewer aftershocks, as a finite-fault study of 1990-2017 events (Dascher-Cousineau et al. 2020) suggested? Approach: we measured durations from 4,364 SCARDEC source time functions (1992-2024) and counted USGS ComCat M4.5+ events within max(40 km, 2 rupture lengths) in 30 days after 1,634 declustered shallow (depth 50 km or less) Mw 6.0+ mainshocks. Negative binomial models controlled magnitude, depth, faulting style, background rate, period and plate-boundary setting. Results: in the planned pooled test, the count ratio per 10 times higher proxy was 1.03 (95% CI 0.94-1.13), and 0.94 (0.74-1.20) for 2018-2024 events. The proxy gave no held-out log-score gain. In an exploratory split, slopes had opposite signs (interaction p = 0.0001): thrust 0.78 (0.68-0.90; interface-like 0.72; 2018-2024 0.68, 0.46-1.00) and strike-slip 1.24 (1.07-1.43; oceanic transforms 1.49). The signs held in 16 robustness variants, but with 20-degree cell fixed effects the thrust slope became 0.90 (0.78-1.04), so part of it is regional. The proxy did not explain the strike-slip aftershock deficit, and separate slopes gave no clear held-out forecast gain (+0.0025 nats per event, CI -0.016 to +0.019). Limitations: teleseismic duration is a noisy proxy that also contains rupture shape and velocity; ComCat completeness varies; the faulting-style split was added after the first results.
